# Darkroom Film Developing

## Overview

I develop black and white film at the kitchen sink, with a tank and a dark bag, and the whole process takes about half an hour once the chemistry is at temperature. Ilford HP5+ is the film I use most, because it is forgiving and it suits the dull light I usually shoot in. I develop it in Rodinal at 1+50, which gives a slightly grainy, sharp look I like. The routine is fixed and I do not improvise, because the chemistry rewards consistency. The number that matters to me is the one I have printed on the wall above the sink: 11 minutes at 20 C. Everything else follows from getting the temperature right and the timing right. I do not develop colour, and I do not push the film, because the dull light I usually shoot in does not ask for it and a pushed roll is harder to read if something goes wrong. What I like about this process is that it is entirely mechanical. There is no screen and no firmware and nothing to update, just a tank, a thermometer, and a clock, and the result depends on how carefully I follow the three numbers written above the sink. A roll that comes out well is a roll that came out well because I did the boring thing correctly, and that is the whole appeal.

## Steps

I start by bringing the chemistry to temperature. The developer, the stop bath, and the rapid fixer all need to be at 20 C, so I stand the bottles in a sink of water and check them with a thermometer until they settle. A couple of degrees out changes the development, so I wait rather than guess. While the water warms I load the film into the tank in the dark bag, which I do by feel: the spiral takes the film, and a click at the end tells me it is properly seated.

When everything is at temperature I pour in the developer and start the clock. For HP5+ in Rodinal at 1+50 the time is 11 minutes at 20 C. For the first 30 seconds I agitate continuously, turning the tank upside down and back, then I set it down and tap it to dislodge any bubbles. After that first burst I agitate for 5 seconds every minute, which is the rhythm I keep for the rest of the development. I pour the developer out a few seconds before the time is up so it is fully drained by the 11 minute mark.

Then the stop bath. I fill the tank and agitate for a moment to halt the development, then pour it out. The stop is quick and it protects the fixer that follows, so I never skip it. Then the rapid fixer for 4 minutes, with the same slow agitation rhythm, which clears the unexposed silver and makes the film safe to look at in the light. I pour the fixer back into its bottle, because it can be reused several times.

Next comes the wash. I wash the film for 5 minutes with a drop of wetting agent in the final rinse, which stops water marks drying onto the surface. The wash matters more than people expect, because fixer left in the emulsion will stain the negatives in a few years. Then I hang the film to dry in the shower, clipped at both ends with a weighted clip at the bottom, and I leave the room for a few hours so nothing settles on it while it is wet.

## Troubleshooting

The most common fault is a thin negative, which usually means the developer was too cold or the time was too short. Before I blame the film or the meter I check the thermometer was in the developer, not in the water beside it. A dense negative is the opposite and is normally overdevelopment, which on this film is usually a temperature a few degrees high rather than a timing mistake. Streaks along the length of the film point to uneven agitation, often a tank that was not inverted far enough on the first minute. Bubbles that leave small marks come from not tapping the tank after the first agitation. A cloudy or milky film after fixing means the fixer is exhausted, and I mix a fresh batch rather than trying to push the old one further. Dust on the dried negative is almost always a room problem, so I hang the film somewhere the air is still. A film that comes out blank along its whole length is the one that hurts, and it is almost always a camera fault rather than a development one, so I check the shutter before I blame the chemistry. A single frame with a hard edge usually means the film was not loaded flat in the spiral and two frames touched. A light leak that shows up as a fogged strip down one side is usually the tank lid not being fully seated, and a quick check of the lid before every pour costs nothing.

## Notes

The single biggest improvement I made was writing the numbers on the wall and never changing them. Consistency beats cleverness here. I mix fresh fixer every few rolls rather than trusting it forever, and I keep the developer in a dark bottle with a squeeze of air out of it so it does not oxidise between sessions. The thermometer lives in a drawer beside the tank, because a missing thermometer is the reason people guess the temperature. If I photograph something worth printing I develop it the same week, since the roll in the camera is the one I am most likely to lose. The film I have not shot yet is the film that is at risk, so I keep one roll loaded and develop it as soon as it is done. I mix fresh chemistry in small batches rather than making a large bottle last, because an old developer gives results that vary from roll to roll and makes it impossible to tell a mistake in the tank from a mistake in the storage.
